title: Build Your First Blockchain DApp
tagline: Plan, write, test, deploy and ship an on-chain guestbook, with every code listing compiled and checked
summary: A guided build of a complete decentralised application: plan it, write and test the Guestbook contract, deploy it to a test network with Hardhat, connect a plain-JavaScript front end with ethers, design the transaction states and ship it safely. The Solidity compiles with solc and the JavaScript passes a syntax check; you run everything yourself on your own computer with a test wallet. Labs check your planning, reading, design and review work.

modules.title: Plan the dApp
modules.summary: Choosing a small idea, writing user stories and sketching the architecture before writing code.
modules.outcome: You can scope a small dApp, divide the work between contract, front end and tooling and set up a sensible project layout.
modules.intro: The fastest way to learn Web3 development is to build one small thing all the way through. In this course you will build an on-chain guestbook: a contract that stores short messages and a web page where anyone with a wallet can read and post them. Before writing code, we plan.

topics.title: Choosing a good first project
topics.html:
A good first dApp is small enough to finish in a weekend and complete enough to teach every layer. It has one contract with a handful of functions, one page, a wallet connection and an event.

Good first ideas and why
IdeaWhat it teaches
Guestbook (this course)Storing data, events, input limits, reading lists, rendering user content safely
Tip jarReceiving and withdrawing ETH
Voting boardMappings, one-vote rules and access control
Certificate verifierHashes on-chain and files off-chain
Simple crowdfundDeadlines, refunds and state machines
Signs of a project that is too big
SignFix
Needs its own token and a marketLeave tokens for later courses
Needs random numbers or price feedsChoose an idea without outside data
Needs user accounts and private dataKeep private data off-chain; start without it
Needs upgrades or governanceShip v1 immutable

Check what you just learned

1. Why choose a small first project?
  • It is boring
  • It earns more
  • You can finish it and learn every layer (correct)
  • Large projects are illegal

Completing the loop teaches the most.

Tip

Write down the one sentence that describes your dApp: 'Anyone can ___ so that ___.' If you cannot, narrow the idea.

Check what you just learned

1. A good first dApp needs:
  • A custom token and an exchange
  • Price oracles
  • Machine learning
  • One contract and one page (correct)

Keep it small.
keyPoints: Pick a small idea you can finish; complete the whole loop.
Avoid tokens, outside data and upgrades in a first project.

topics.html:
User stories for the guestbook
As aI wantSo that
Visitorto read the latest messagesI can see who has signed
Wallet ownerto post a short messageI leave my mark on the chain
Readernew messages to appear without reloadingthe page feels alive
Our tool choices
NeedToolWhy
Write, compile, test and deploy contractsHardhatMature, JavaScript-based, local test chain
Talk to the chain from JavaScriptethers (version 6)A small, widely used library
WalletAny browser wallet that supports the standard window.ethereum interfaceUsers bring their own

Project layout

  • contracts/ holds Guestbook.sol.
  • test/ holds the tests.
  • scripts/ holds the deploy script.
  • frontend/ holds index.html and app.js.
  • hardhat.config.js, package.json and .env (never committed).

Check what you just learned

1. What belongs in the .env file?
  • The deployer key and RPC URL, which are secrets (correct)
  • The front-end code
  • The README
  • The tests

And .env must be in .gitignore.

Check what you just learned

1. Which tool runs your tests on a local chain?
  • A wallet
  • Hardhat (correct)
  • A browser
  • A bank

A development environment.
keyPoints: Write user stories, then sketch contract, wallet, RPC and page.
Use Hardhat, ethers, a plain page and a test network.

topics.title: Setting up the tools
topics.html:
You need Node.js (a current long-term-support version), a code editor and a browser wallet. The commands below create a Hardhat project. They run on your own computer; this platform does not run code, so follow along locally.

Setup steps

  1. Install Node.js and check with node --version.
  2. Create a folder and run npm init -y.
  3. Install Hardhat and its toolbox with npm install --save-dev hardhat @nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox.
  4. Install dotenv with npm install dotenv for loading secrets.
  5. Run npx hardhat init and choose a JavaScript project.
  6. Delete the sample contract and create contracts/Guestbook.sol.
Watch out

Package versions and commands change. Follow the current Hardhat documentation if a step differs from what you see, and pin the versions you use in package.json.

What each package does
PackageJob
hardhatCompile, test, run a local chain and deploy
@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolboxA bundle with ethers, Chai matchers and more
dotenvLoads the .env file into process.env

Check what you just learned

1. Why pin package versions?
  • To save disk space
  • Because npm requires it
  • So your project builds the same way later (correct)
  • To hide code

APIs change between versions.

Check what you just learned

1. dotenv is used to:
  • Compile Solidity
  • Style the page
  • Send ETH
  • Load secrets from a .env file (correct)

Keeps secrets out of the code.

Key terms: flip and sort

dApp
A decentralised application
Hardhat
A development environment for Ethereum
ethers
A JavaScript library for Ethereum
RPC
How apps talk to nodes
User story
A short description of a need from a user's view
.env
A file holding secrets for a project
keyPoints: Install Node.js, Hardhat and dotenv and start a JavaScript project.
Pin versions and follow current documentation.

modules.title: Write and test the contract
modules.summary: The Guestbook contract, line by line, with a test suite that checks the rules.
modules.outcome: You can explain every part of the Guestbook, write tests for happy and failing paths and estimate the cost of storing data.
modules.intro: The contract is the heart of the dApp: it holds the rules that nobody can bypass. We write it small, with limits, and test it before anything else is built on top.

topics.title: The Guestbook contract
topics.html:
Design decisions
DecisionReason
Entry struct with author, message and timestampGroups one post's data
MAX_LENGTH of 140 bytesLimits storage cost and abuse
Custom errors EmptyMessage and TooLongCheap, clear failures
Posted event with indexed author and idThe front end can follow and filter posts
latest(limit) returns at most 50 entriesA read that cannot grow without limit
entries is private and has no delete functionPosts are permanent; there is no admin to abuse

Notice what is missing: no owner, no editing and no deleting. That keeps the contract simple and trustworthy, but it also means a posted message stays forever, so the front end must be careful what it asks users to publish.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does latest() cap the number of entries it returns?
  • So a read never becomes too large as the list grows (correct)
  • To hide data
  • To save storage
  • Because mappings require it

Bounded work.

Check what you just learned

1. A message of 141 bytes causes:
  • A success
  • A revert with TooLong (correct)
  • A fee refund
  • A new event

The limit is 140.
keyPoints: The contract is small, bounded and without admin powers.
Posted data is permanent.

topics.title: Testing the contract
topics.html:
What the tests cover
TestWhy
Posting stores a message and emits the event with the right argumentsThe happy path and the event the front end relies on
Empty and over-long messages revert with the correct errorThe input limits
latest() never returns more than 50 entries and returns the newestThe bound and the ordering

Run the tests with npx hardhat test. A passing result means these specific rules hold. It does not prove the contract is perfect, so add tests whenever you think of a new case, and especially for each bug you ever find.

More tests worth adding

  • A message of exactly 140 bytes succeeds.
  • Two different accounts can both post.
  • count() increases by one for each post.
  • latest(0) returns an empty list.
  • A multi-byte character message is limited by bytes, not characters.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test a message of exactly 140 bytes?
  • It is trivial
  • It costs less
  • Edge values are where off-by-one bugs hide (correct)
  • Required by law

Boundaries matter.

Check what you just learned

1. Tests prove:
  • The contract is perfect
  • Nothing
  • The contract is audited
  • The tested rules hold (correct)

Only what they check.
keyPoints: Tests check the happy path, the failures and the bounds.
Add a test for every edge and every bug.

topics.title: What storing data costs
topics.html:
Every message written to storage costs gas, and the cost grows with its length because storage is charged per 32-byte slot. A 20-byte greeting fits in one slot, a 140-byte message needs five, and a 1,000-byte note needs thirty-two.

Formula · A rough cost model

gas ≈ 21,000 + (slots × 22,100) + about 70,000 for the other fields and event

Slots = message length ÷ 32, rounded up.

Cost of a post

Change the message length, gas price and ETH price to see the rough gas and cost. This is a teaching model, not a quote.

Adjust Message length (bytes), Gas price (gwei), ETH price (rupees) and see Slots used, Rough gas, Rough cost (rupees) change.

Watch out

If you let users store unlimited text, you let them waste their own money, but you also let them fill the chain with junk that every node must carry. Always set limits.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does a longer message cost more?
  • It needs more 32-byte storage slots (correct)
  • It is slower
  • It uses more events
  • It has a higher gas price

Storage is charged per slot.

Check what you just learned

1. A 140-byte message needs about:
  • 1 slot
  • 5 slots (correct)
  • 32 slots
  • 0 slots

140 divided by 32, rounded up.

Key terms: flip and sort

Struct
A custom record type
Custom error
A cheap named failure
Indexed event argument
A searchable log field
Test suite
A set of automated checks
Edge case
A value at the boundary of a rule
Storage slot
A 32-byte unit of contract storage
keyPoints: Storage is charged per 32-byte slot.
Set length limits to protect users and the chain.

modules.title: Deploy to a test network
modules.summary: Local chain, configuration, secrets, the deployment script and verification.
modules.outcome: You can configure Hardhat for a test network, deploy safely and record the address and source for your front end.
modules.intro: Deployment turns your code into a live contract at an address. Done carelessly, it is also where private keys leak. This module shows the safe, repeatable way.

topics.title: Configuration and secrets
topics.html:
The configuration reads the RPC URL and the deployer key from environment variables, so no secret appears in the code. Your .env file looks like this (with your own values), and it must be listed in .gitignore:

Rules for secrets

  1. Use a brand-new wallet with only test ETH for deployment.
  2. Never reuse a key that controls real funds.
  3. Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.
  4. Never paste keys into chats, tickets or screenshots.
  5. If a key leaks, treat it as compromised: stop using it and move anything it held.
Watch out

Automated scanners watch public code repositories for private keys and drain them within minutes. A key committed even once should be considered lost.

Check what you just learned

1. Where should the deployer key be stored?
  • In hardhat.config.js
  • In the README
  • In a .env file listed in .gitignore (correct)
  • In the contract

Keep it out of the code and out of git.

Check what you just learned

1. A leaked private key should be treated as:
  • Fine
  • Public information only
  • Encrypted
  • Compromised (correct)

Replace it.
keyPoints: Load secrets from environment variables; never commit them.
Use a separate, test-only deployer wallet.

topics.title: The deploy script
topics.html:
Running it
CommandWhat it does
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.jsDeploys to Hardhat's in-memory network; good for a quick check
npx hardhat nodeStarts a persistent local chain with funded test accounts
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network localhostDeploys to that local chain
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network sepoliaDeploys to the Sepolia test network using your .env settings
Tip

Write the deployed address into a small JSON file or the README each time. You will need it for the front end and for anyone who wants to check your work.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the deploy script print that the front end needs?
  • The contract address (correct)
  • The private key
  • The nonce
  • The fee

The page needs to know where the contract lives.

Check what you just learned

1. The first place to run a deploy script is:
  • The main network
  • A local chain (correct)
  • A friend's wallet
  • A bank

Cheap and quick.
keyPoints: Deploy locally first, then to a test network with a faucet-funded key.
Record the contract address.

topics.title: Verifying the source
topics.html:
A deployed contract is just bytecode. To let people read what it does, you publish the source code and compiler settings to a block explorer, which recompiles it and checks that the result matches the deployed bytecode. This is called verification.

Why verify
BenefitDetail
TrustUsers can read exactly what the contract does
ConvenienceExplorers show readable functions and let users call them
ReviewAuditors and curious users can check your work
ToolsWallets and indexers can decode events and errors

Hardhat has a verification plugin that does this from the command line with the contract address and constructor arguments. Explorer websites also offer a form where you paste your source. Whichever you use, record the exact compiler version and settings.

Common mistakes

  • Verifying with different compiler settings than you deployed with, which fails.
  • Forgetting constructor arguments.
  • Not verifying and then asking users to trust an unreadable contract.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a block explorer do when you verify a contract?
  • Changes the contract
  • Moves the funds
  • Recompiles your source and checks it matches the deployed bytecode (correct)
  • Sets the fee

It proves the source matches.

Check what you just learned

1. Verified source lets users:
  • Edit the contract
  • Skip gas
  • Mint tokens
  • Read what the contract really does (correct)

Transparency.

Key terms: flip and sort

Faucet
A site giving free test ETH
Deployer
The account that deploys a contract
Network config
Settings for a chain in Hardhat
Verification
Publishing matching source code
Environment variable
A setting passed to a program from outside
Private key
The secret that controls an account
keyPoints: Verification publishes source that provably matches the deployed bytecode.
Record compiler settings and constructor arguments.

modules.title: Connect the front end
modules.summary: Connecting a wallet, reading the chain and sending a transaction from a web page.
modules.outcome: You can connect a wallet, check the network, read from and write to a contract with ethers and handle errors gracefully.
modules.intro: The page is where users meet your contract. It must connect to their wallet, make sure they are on the right network, read data for them and ask for their signature to write, always in clear language.

topics.title: The page and the script
topics.html:
The front end is two small files. The HTML defines the interface; the JavaScript module connects to the wallet and the contract. Study the page first: it has a connect button, a status line that screen readers announce, a form and a list for messages.

Notice the accessibility details: the form field has a label, the status line has role="status" so changes are announced, and everything works with a keyboard.

Check what you just learned

1. Why give the status element role="status"?
  • So assistive technology announces changes (correct)
  • For colour
  • To store data
  • For speed

Everyone should know what is happening.

Tip

Open index.html through a simple local web server rather than by double-clicking it, because browsers restrict some features for local files. Hardhat is not needed for this; any static server works.

Check what you just learned

1. A label on the message input helps:
  • Only designers
  • Screen reader users and everyone clicking the label (correct)
  • Nobody
  • Gas

Basic accessibility.
keyPoints: The page has a connect button, a status line, a form and a list.
Use labels and live regions so it is accessible.

topics.title: Connecting and reading
topics.html:
Walking through the script
PartWhat it does
BrowserProvider(window.ethereum)Wraps the wallet's standard connection
provider.send("eth_requestAccounts", [])Asks the wallet to let the page see an account; the user must approve
provider.getNetwork() and the chain id checkMakes sure the wallet is on Sepolia (chain id 11155111) before doing anything
getSigner()Gets the connected account, which can sign
new Contract(ADDRESS, ABI, signer)A handle that turns JavaScript calls into encoded transactions and reads
guestbook.latest(20)A read: free and instant
guestbook.on("Posted", refresh)Listens for the event and refreshes the list
li.textContent = ...Shows the message as plain text, never as HTML
Definition

Human-readable ABI. ethers lets you list only the functions and events you need as readable strings instead of the full JSON ABI. That keeps the page small and the code easy to read.

Watch out

Pin the version of ethers in the import URL to the one you tested, and check the current documentation. APIs and CDN paths change over time.

Check what you just learned

1. What does eth_requestAccounts do?
  • Sends ETH
  • Deploys a contract
  • Asks the wallet to share an account with the page, after user approval (correct)
  • Signs a message

Connecting requires consent.

Check what you just learned

1. A provider in ethers is:
  • A signature
  • A fee
  • A token
  • A connection to the network or wallet (correct)

It is how the page reaches the chain.
keyPoints: Provider, signer and contract are the three objects of ethers.
Always check the network and render text safely.

topics.title: Writing and handling errors
topics.html:
Reading is free and instant; writing needs the user's approval and takes time. The post function in the script shows the complete life of a write: ask, wait for the wallet, wait for the network, report success or failure.

Errors and what to tell the user
What happenedHow it shows in codeMessage
User cancelled in the walleterror.code is ACTION_REJECTEDYou cancelled the transaction. Nothing was sent.
Contract rejected the inputA custom error such as TooLong in the error dataYour message is too long. Please use 140 characters or fewer.
Wrong networkChain id check failsPlease switch to the Sepolia test network.
Not enough ETH for gasInsufficient funds errorYou need a little test ETH to pay the network fee.
Network troubleTimeout or connection errorWe could not reach the network. Please try again.

Common mistakes

  • Showing raw error text such as 'execution reverted' to ordinary users.
  • Treating a cancelled transaction as a failure.
  • Not disabling the Post button while a transaction is pending, which allows double posting.

Check what you just learned

1. How should the page treat a user cancelling in the wallet?
  • As a normal choice, with a calm message (correct)
  • As a bug to report
  • By retrying automatically
  • By crashing

Cancelling is not an error.

Check what you just learned

1. To prevent double posting you should:
  • Hide the wallet
  • Disable the button while a transaction is pending (correct)
  • Increase gas
  • Reload the page

One action at a time.

Key terms: flip and sort

Provider
A connection to a node or wallet
Signer
An account that can sign
Contract object
A JavaScript handle for a deployed contract
Chain id
A number identifying a network
ABI
The interface description of a contract
EIP-1193
The standard wallet interface that window.ethereum follows
keyPoints: A write has several steps; show each.
Translate errors into plain language and treat cancel as normal.

modules.title: Events, UX and states
modules.summary: Making the page feel alive and trustworthy: live updates, clear states, formatting and accessibility.
modules.outcome: You can follow events for live updates, design clear states for each stage of a transaction and make the page accessible.
modules.intro: Blockchains are slow and sometimes unpredictable. The difference between a dApp people trust and one they abandon is how well it explains what is happening. This module is about those details.

topics.title: Live updates with events
topics.html:
Instead of asking the chain again and again whether anything changed, the page can subscribe to the contract's Posted event. When anyone posts, the event arrives and the page refreshes. The same pattern powers dashboards, notifications and activity feeds across Web3.

Reading history versus listening
ApproachUse when
Call a view function such as latest()Showing the current state when the page loads
Query past eventsBuilding a history from a known block number
Subscribe to new eventsKeeping the page up to date while it is open
Use an indexer serviceLarge histories, search and analytics

Good habits

  1. Load the current list first, then listen for new events.
  2. Remember the page can miss events if the connection drops; refresh on reconnect.
  3. Avoid duplicates: use the event's id to skip entries you already show.
  4. Limit how many entries you hold in memory.

Check what you just learned

1. What should the page do first when it loads?
  • Wait for an event
  • Delete the list
  • Load the current list, then subscribe to new events (correct)
  • Ask the user to refresh

Current state first.

Check what you just learned

1. An indexer is useful for:
  • Tiny histories
  • Hashing
  • Signing
  • Large histories and search (correct)

Raw logs get unwieldy.
keyPoints: Load current state, then subscribe to events.
Handle dropped connections and duplicates.

topics.title: Designing the states
topics.html:
The states of a write
StateWhat the user seesNext
IdleA ready formUser presses Post
SigningA message: Waiting for you to confirm in your walletApprove or cancel
PendingA message: Sent. Waiting for confirmation, with a link to the explorerA block includes it
ConfirmedA message: Posted, and the new entry appearsIdle
FailedA clear reason and a button to try againIdle
CancelledA calm note that nothing was sentIdle

How long should the spinner last?

Change the block time and the number of blocks expected to see how long the wait is, and when to show a 'taking longer than usual' hint.

Adjust Average block time (seconds), Blocks expected before inclusion and see Typical wait (seconds), Show a hint after (seconds) change.

Tip

Always show the transaction hash with a link to a block explorer once it exists. It lets users check the status themselves and reduces support questions.

Check what you just learned

1. What should the page show if the transaction is pending for a long time?
  • A hint that it is taking longer and a link to the explorer (correct)
  • Nothing
  • An error that it failed
  • A new form

Honest, helpful waiting.

Check what you just learned

1. Cancelled in the wallet is best shown as:
  • A crash
  • A calm note that nothing was sent (correct)
  • A fee
  • A success

No harm done.
keyPoints: Design idle, signing, pending, confirmed, failed and cancelled states.
Show the hash and an explorer link while pending.

topics.title: Formatting, accessibility and trust
topics.html:
Presenting blockchain data to humans
DataShow it as
AddressA short form such as 0x12ab…89ef, with a copy button and a link to the explorer
Amount in weiETH with sensible decimals; never raw wei
TimestampA local, readable date and 'x minutes ago'
Transaction hashShort with a link
NetworkA clear name and a warning if wrong

Accessibility checklist

  • Every control is reachable and operable by keyboard.
  • Status changes are announced with a live region.
  • Text has enough contrast and does not rely on colour alone.
  • Buttons say what they do: 'Post message', not just 'Submit'.
  • Error messages say what to do next.
  • The page works on a phone screen.
Watch out

A dApp page asks users to trust it with their wallet. Never ask for more permission than needed, never auto-open wallet popups on page load, and show exactly what each request does.

Check what you just learned

1. Why show amounts in ETH rather than wei?
  • Wei is illegal
  • ETH is faster
  • Humans cannot read 18-digit numbers easily (correct)
  • Wei is hidden

Use human units.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a trust-building habit?
  • Auto-opening wallet popups
  • Asking for unlimited approvals
  • Hiding addresses
  • Explaining each request before the wallet appears (correct)

Be clear and minimal.

Key terms: flip and sort

Event subscription
Listening for new logs from a contract
Indexer
A service that organises on-chain events for queries
Live region
An element whose changes screen readers announce
Pending state
A transaction sent but not yet included
Confirmation
A block built on the one with your transaction
Explorer link
A link to view a transaction on a block explorer
keyPoints: Format addresses, amounts and times for humans.
Make the page accessible and never ask for more permission than needed.

modules.title: Ship it and keep it secure
modules.summary: Hosting the front end, protecting users from common attacks and keeping an eye on the contract after launch.
modules.outcome: You can host a static front end, protect it against cross-site scripting and phishing risks and write a launch and monitoring plan.
modules.intro: A dApp is only as safe as its weakest part. The contract may be perfect and the page can still hurt users. This final module covers hosting, front-end security and the habits that keep a live project healthy.

topics.title: Hosting the front end
topics.html:
Options for hosting a static page
OptionProsCons
A static hosting serviceSimple, fast, free tiers, HTTPSA company controls the host
Your own web serverFull controlYou maintain it
IPFS with a gateway or nameContent-addressed and hard to censorUpdates need new addresses or name records; users may need a gateway
Both: a normal site and an IPFS copyRedundancyTwo things to keep in step

Hosting checklist

  1. Serve over HTTPS only.
  2. Put the contract address and network name on the page, with a link to the verified source.
  3. Pin your dependencies and avoid loading scripts from unknown sites.
  4. Keep the deployed files in version control so you can compare what is live.
  5. Set up a way for users to contact you.
Watch out

Phishing sites copy popular dApps and trick people into signing malicious transactions. Make your official address easy to find and tell users to bookmark it.

Check what you just learned

1. What should every dApp page be served over?
  • HTTPS (correct)
  • HTTP
  • FTP
  • Email

Encryption and integrity for the page.

Check what you just learned

1. Phishing dApps are a risk because:
  • They are faster
  • They copy real sites to trick users into signing harmful transactions (correct)
  • They are free
  • They use gas

Users must check addresses.
keyPoints: Static hosting is simple; IPFS is more censorship-resistant but harder to update.
Serve over HTTPS and publish the official address.

topics.title: Front-end security
topics.html:
Because the Guestbook shows messages written by strangers, it must treat every message as untrusted. If the page inserted messages as HTML, a malicious message such as an image tag with a script handler could run code in every visitor's browser, next to their wallet. This is cross-site scripting (XSS).

Safe and unsafe
UnsafeSafe
element.innerHTML = messageelement.textContent = message
Building HTML strings from user textCreating elements with document.createElement and setting textContent

More habits

  • Content Security Policy headers where your host allows them.
  • No private keys, ever, in front-end code.
  • Show the exact action, contract and amount before asking for a signature.
  • Warn users about approvals and let them revoke old ones.
  • Keep dependencies updated and review changes.

1. Why is element.innerHTML = message dangerous for user messages?
  • It is slow

topics.title: After launch: monitor and maintain
topics.html:
What to watch
ThingHow
Contract activitySubscribe to events; alert on unusual spikes
Page availabilityAn uptime monitor that checks the page and the RPC provider
DependenciesSecurity advisories for packages you use
AbuseSpam or offensive messages in a permanent guestbook: decide in advance what the page will filter or hide
User reportsA contact address and a clear process

A permanent, open contract makes moderation interesting. The chain keeps everything, but your page need not show everything. A common design is to let the page hide messages from a blocklist maintained off-chain, while the contract stays neutral. Decide your policy and publish it.

A launch-day routine

  1. Test the live page from a clean browser profile.
  2. Post and read a message yourself on the test network.
  3. Check the explorer shows the verified source.
  4. Share the link with a few testers first.
  5. Write down what you will do if something goes wrong.
Watch out

This course teaches building on a test network. Anything involving real money needs far more testing, an independent audit and legal advice.

Check what you just learned

1. How can a page deal with offensive messages stored on a permanent chain?
  • Choose not to display them, using a published policy (correct)
  • Delete them from the chain
  • Ignore all messages
  • Shut down the chain

The chain keeps data; the page chooses what to show.

Check what you just learned

1. On a permanent chain, moderation usually means:
  • Deleting data
  • Choosing what the page displays (correct)
  • Rewriting history
  • Banning the chain

The page filters; the chain does not.
